headline: The Bunker Are Home: Dawn Blitzes at the Point, Bass Pushing 30 Pounds
subhead: Full moon tide has pinned the bait against the boulders — and the striper fishing at Montauk is doing what it's supposed to do in the second week of August.
body_markdown:
There's a stretch of the calendar, usually the first two weeks of August, when Montauk stops being a fishery and becomes a machine. The bunker come home to the south side in numbers that blacken the water off the Lighthouse, the terns and gannets find them at first light, and everything that swims with a spine east of Shagwong knows exactly where breakfast is. We're in that window right now, and I'd argue we've been in it for about ten days straight.

I was out at 5:15 Tuesday morning, running the boat along the boulder field off the Point in maybe eighteen feet of water, and the whole south side was doing what it does when a big moon pulls a big tide — bait balled up tight against the rocks, refusing to leave, and stripers using the current to pin it there. This full moon has been generous. Water's holding around 76 degrees on the ocean side, which isn't classic bass water on paper, but the current is so strong right now that it's kept the fish feeding hard on the moving stages rather than sulking deep through the heat. That's the story of this whole week — strong tide, low light, bunker schools doing the work.

The pattern at North Bar has been the same three mornings running: bunker spoons and 2-ounce bucktails worked just under the surface on the last hour of the incoming, into the first hour of the outgoing, right where the rip stands up over that boulder structure. We've had bass to 28 and 30 pounds on topwater plugs — the big pencil poppers and Danny-style swimmers — when the fish are up and slashing, and switched to bucktails tipped with a strip of bunker belly when they slide down a few feet. Shagwong Reef has been holding fish too, though it's been more of a bluefish show there this week — jumbo blues in the 8 to 12 pound class mixed right into the bass schools, which means wire leaders or you're donating plugs to the bottom. Turtle Cove has fished better on the last two hours of daylight than at dawn, which tells me the bait's shifting position with the tide swing rather than sitting still — worth knowing if you're planning your morning around one spot.

Night fishing has held up too, and if you want a shot at something heavier than the daylight schoolies, that's still the play. Eels drifted slow along the boulder field on the building tide, fished tight to the rocks in the dark, have produced some of the better fish of the week — nothing I'd call a 50, but a handful in the 30s came off that pattern for guys willing to stay out past midnight. That low-light window matters more now than it did in June. Peak-summer heat pushes these fish into a strict schedule — dawn, dusk, full dark — and daytime action outside the current-swept structure has been thin. Don't waste a midday tide on flat, sunny water expecting a repeat of what happened at 5 a.m.

Fluke fishing has been the more dependable, less dramatic story. Lake Montauk's west basin has been giving up keeper fluke to 4 and 5 pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and chartreuse bucktails, drifted slow over the sand-and-eelgrass bottom on the outgoing as the lake drains through the inlet. The channel edge off Star Island jetty has done the same on that same ebb — deeper water, stronger current, bigger average fish, but you're fighting boat traffic through the harbor mouth. Porgies remain the honest man's fishery on Shagwong and the reef structure off the Point — small hooks, sandworms or clam, straight up-and-down in 25 to 40 feet, and you'll fill a bucket without much drama. That fishery doesn't get the ink the bass blitzes do, but it's about as close to a sure thing as this month offers.

What hasn't showed yet, and I get asked about it every single day at the dock, is albies and bonito. We flagged this water as the one to watch closest going into August, and the ocean-side temps have crept into that trigger range — but the switch hasn't flipped. Nobody I trust has iron in the boat yet off the Point or in the rips. That first wave typically shows in the final weeks of August, and with the surface temps sitting where they are, I don't think we're far off. Keep a light spinning rod rigged with a small epoxy jig or a Deadly Dick in the rocket launcher when you're running bunker spoons — you don't want to be digging through a rod locker the morning they finally show up busting bait on the surface east of the Point.

Looking ahead, this moon's grip on the tide will start to ease over the next few days, and the bite windows should settle back into a more normal rhythm rather than the exaggerated dawn-and-dusk blitzes we've had. If the wind stays out of the west and the bunker schools hold their position along the south side, I'd keep working North Bar and the boulder field on the moving water — that's still the highest-percentage play on the Point right now. If the bunker push east toward Shagwong, follow them. They're driving this whole show, and they have been for two weeks straight.
